wide_select.schema: t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, n INTEGER, s TEXT, w TEXT ~1KB, b BLOB ~100B)
wide_select.timed_sql: SELECT n, s, w, b FROM t
wide_select.path_confirmed: real pager+VDBE (execute_with_borrowed_bindings_internal, BtCursor::advance_next, decode_value_with_encoding) - NOT the memdb SimpleFullTableScan shortcut

bulk_insert.schema: ins(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, n INTEGER, s TEXT, w TEXT ~1KB, b BLOB ~100B) no secondary index

select_top_self_pct.note: blob cache-clone = O(1) Arc bump, no memcpy

select_top_inclusive_pct.sym: std::..::Once::call (OnceLock::get_or_init for the wide-text cache-clone Arc<str>)

biggest_optimizable_hotspot.name: Redundant per-row Arc<str> allocation from the wide-column cache-clone in column_to_reg_direct
chain: engine.rs:16139 decode_column_from_offset_reuse_with_encoding -> hint-miss on distinct-per-row text -> HeapOwned{String, OnceLock::new()} (value.rs:281); String buffer is pool-reused so decode is ~alloc-free

engine.rs:16159 cache_decoded(payload_idx, val.clone()) -> SmallTextRepr::clone (value.rs:254) runs Arc::clone(shared.get_or_init(|| Arc::from(text))) = fresh ~1KB Arc<str> malloc + 1KB memcpy EVERY row
record.rs:1016 cache_decoded pool-returns the prior slot; the cached Arc<str> is never read by a single-pass scan and is freed next row
biggest_optimizable_hotspot.why_optimizable: returning 1KB text needs ONE owned copy (irreducible); engine currently makes TWO (pooled decode String + defensive cache-clone Arc<str>). BLOB columns are unaffected (Arc<[u8]> clone is O(1) bump).
biggest_optimizable_hotspot.evidence: Once::call inclusive 9.67% (Vec) / 3.66% (stream); feeds top self leaves __memcpy_avx_unaligned_erms and _int_malloc

second_lever_result_set_accumulation.finding: query() keeps all 300K wide rows (~330MB) live before return -> glibc arena grow/return churn (brk 4.5%, munmap 2.6%, sbrk/systrim/morecore ~12% incl). Allocator self-time collapses 36.7%->9.6% when streaming.
second_lever_result_set_accumulation.classification: API-shaped, not engine-shaped: streaming for_each already avoids it and is 2.06x faster (1689 vs 3479 ns/row).
